newsitem.title: ISRAEL: 18 killed in Jerusalem market bomb blasts.
newsitem.headline: 18 killed in Jerusalem market bomb blasts.

text.p: Eighteen people were killed on Wednesday when two explosions tore through a crowded outdoor market in Jewish West Jerusalem.
Police said the attack was apparently the work of Moslem militant suicide bombers.
The bombings, within seconds of each other, were by far the deadliest attack in Israel since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's election 14 months ago.
They occurred on the eve of a visit by U.S. envoy Dennis Ross for talks with Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on ways to revive their stalled peace process.
"We're looking at 18 dead right now but that's not the final figure. The attack was apparently carried out by two suicide bombers," Israel's police chief Assaf Hefetz told reporters.
He said authorities had imposed a closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip, barring Palestinians from entering Israel.
The bombers, who police said had carried the bombs into parallel streets in the Mahane Yehuda market about 40 metres (yards) apart, were apparently among the dead.
Israel Radio said wigs had been found near their bodies, suggesting they had put on disguises. Israelis gathered at the scene of the attack shouting "Death to Arabs", it said.
Arafat called Israeli President Ezer Weizman and Netanyahu to express his condolences for the dead, a statement from the Palestinian leader's office said.
Blood mingled with pulverised fruit and vegetables strewn on the ground at the market in one of Jerusalem's busiest areas, where the explosions happened at 1:18 p.m. (1018 GMT).
One man had his leg blown off and another was rushed to an ambulance soaked in blood in a wheelchair. More than 100 people were wounded, Israel Radio quoted an ambulance officer as saying.

Netanyahu, elected in May last year on a pledge to boost security for Israelis, cancelled engagements for later on Wednesday and instead went into crisis talks with his defence and foreign ministers, government officials said.
Witnesses at the market described scenes of carnage and confusion as police, emergency workers and members of the public struggled to remove the dead and cope with the wounded.
"There were two large explosions and then I saw body parts flying in the air. There was a big fireball right in my face," one witness said.
One man in his early 30s who appeared to be paralysed, a market butcher in his smock and rubber boots, lay on the sidewalk on a stretcher as bystanders pleaded for help.
"Why don't they take him? Where is a doctor?" one woman screamed.
Police swiftly closed the market to search through garbage bins and debris for any more bombs.
"The scene here is awful," Israeli Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani told reporters.
The last big bomb blast to rock the Jewish state, on March 21, killed three Israeli women along with the Palestinian bomber, and wounded 42 people at an outdoor cafe in Tel Aviv.
That attack happened three days after Israel broke ground on a Jewish settlement on a hilltop in Arab East Jerusalem known to Israelis as Har Homa and to Palestinians as Jabal Abu Ghneim.
Israeli-Palestinian peace talks have been in crisis since then, with Arafat insisting substantive talks on a final peace agreement cannot take place until settlement activity stops.

Israel has countered that the Palestinian Authority has failed to meet commitments made under interim peace deals since 1993 to stem violence against Israelis, alleging that some of the Authority's own police are involved in attacks.

"What we are seeing is a lukewarm attempt by the Palestinians to try to portray some cooperation in the field of fighting terror," government spokesman Moshe Fogel told CNN television after Wednesday's attack.

"We need 100 percent cooperation from the Palestinians to fight terror...They cannot on the one hand say that they want peace and on the other hand do nothing, absolutely nothing, to fight terror," he said.
